items.title: Arithmetization of Boolean formulas
items.statement: Over a field F, map constants and variables identically, NOT u to 1-u, AND to uv, OR to u+v-uv. Retain the expression tree; do not expand into monomials.
items.strategy: Recursive construction on formula syntax.

items.title: Arithmetization preserves Boolean values
items.statement: For every Boolean assignment, the arithmetized formula has exactly the original 0/1 value in F.
items.strategy: Check the three gate truth tables, then structural induction.

items.title: Formula degree and point-evaluation cost
items.statement: For a formula with s syntax nodes and t_i occurrences of variable i, its polynomial has individual degree at most t_i and total degree at most sum t_i. Point evaluation takes O(s) field operations.
items.strategy: Induct on the expression tree. Addition takes maximum degree, multiplication adds degree bounds; evaluate nodes once. Constants and the zero polynomial satisfy the upper bounds.

sources.locator: §8.5.1, p.158, 3CNF construction generalized by the same gate induction

items.title: Multilinear extension of a Boolean-cube table
items.statement: An extension of f:{0,1}^n to F is a formal polynomial agreeing with f on the cube; multilinear means degree at most one in every variable. No uniqueness presumed in the definition.
items.strategy: Define the extension relation; theorem below discharges existence and uniqueness.

items.title: Boolean-cube interpolation
items.statement: Every table f:{0,1}^n→F has unique multilinear extension sum_b f(b) product_i [b_i X_i+(1-b_i)(1-X_i)]. Includes n=0 and characteristic two.
items.strategy: The product basis is a delta function on cube vertices. For uniqueness induct using h=(1-X_n)h|0+X_n h|1; zero restrictions imply h=0. Existing polynomial-reduction uniqueness is not reminted.

items.title: Streaming evaluation from a full cube table
items.statement: For a field F and table f:{0,1}^n→F, given all N=2^n indexed values, evaluate the extension at r∈F^n in O(nN) field operations and O(n) field-element storage in one pass (n≥1).
items.strategy: Accumulate each weighted basis term; store r and one accumulator. This is exponential in n, not an efficient oracle for a succinctly specified table.

items.title: Linear-time evaluation from a full cube table
items.statement: For a field F, given the full table f:{0,1}^n→F and r∈F^n, evaluate in O(2^n) field operations and O(2^n+n) storage.
items.strategy: Build basis weights by doubling a prefix table and multiplying by 1-r_i or r_i, then take the finite weighted sum. Geometric sum bounds the work.

items.title: Degree under Boolean elimination operators
items.statement: Write p_b=p|X_i=b. Summation p_0+p_1 preserves remaining individual degree upper bounds; universal product p_0 p_1 and Boolean existential p_0+p_1-p_0p_1 at most double them. Product and Boolean existential have the correct 0/1 semantics; summation is a counting operator, not Boolean OR in arbitrary characteristic.
items.strategy: Degree arithmetic and the already specified AND/OR gates. Repeated products can yield exponential degrees; no claim of efficient quantified-formula verification here.

sources.locator: §8.5.1 p.158 and §8.5.3 opening degree-growth paragraph p.160

items.title: Existing polynomial identity bounds
items.statement: Recall the univariate root bound and multivariate total-degree bound d/|S| for nonempty finite S. Apply them to differences of formal polynomials; total and individual degrees are distinct.
items.strategy: Reuse established item IDs, not the design placeholders thm-polynomial-root-bound or thm-schwartz-zippel-multivariate-form. Explain why sum-check only needs the univariate theorem.

items.title: Sum-check with explicit degree bounds
items.statement: Input: fixed g in n≥1 variables over finite F, trusted individual bounds d_i, claimed H, and trusted point evaluation. Round i receives at most d_i+1 coefficients, checks h_i(0)+h_i(1)=current claim, then draws fresh uniform r_i and updates claim to h_i(r_i). Final comparison is with independently evaluated g(r). Reject malformed messages.
items.strategy: State coefficient representation, message-before-challenge timing and all n rounds, including n=1. Honest h_i is the partial cube sum. H is an input, not an extra counted prover message.

items.title: Perfect completeness of sum-check
items.statement: For true H, the honest partial-sum polynomials satisfy every degree, consistency and terminal check for every challenge sequence.
items.strategy: Finite-sum invariant; substitution and summation cannot increase individual degree.

items.title: A false sum-check claim rarely becomes true
items.statement: Conditioned on any past transcript with a false current claim, either checks reject immediately or the next scalar claim is true with probability at most min(1,d_i/|F|).
items.strategy: Consistency forces h_i to differ from the true partial-sum polynomial. Both degrees ≤d_i and the new challenge is independent of the past; apply root bound to their difference. Becoming true is the exceptional event, not necessarily immediate detection of every false polynomial.

items.title: Adaptive-prover soundness of sum-check
items.statement: For false H, every adaptive prover is accepted with probability at most min(1,sum_i d_i/|F|), hence at most nd/|F| for d_i≤d.
items.strategy: If accepted, an initially false claim must first become true before the trusted terminal equality. Sum the conditional bad-event bounds over n rounds. Fix prover coins or condition on its messages; no independence of round failures is asserted.

items.title: Sum-check verifier resources
items.statement: For n≥1 and D=sum_i(d_i+1), a well-formed transcript uses at most D prover field elements and an arbitrary streamed execution at most D+1; the verifier uses O(D) field operations plus at most one point evaluation, at most n verifier field elements, and at most n samples/rounds. A full execution has n samples/rounds and one terminal evaluation. With b-bit encodings and field-operation cost A(b), bit work is O(D(A(b)+b)) plus evaluation/sampling. Efficient indexed rejection sampling uses expected O(ceil(log2|F|)) bits per sample; for a bijective b-bit encoding with |F|=2^b it uses exactly nb bits.
items.strategy: Stop after the first excess coefficient, use Horner evaluation at 0,1,r_i, and sum message lengths. Polynomial time is conditional on polynomial D, b, evaluator and sampler; the last challenge need not be sent. Uniform sampling has expected O(b) random bits by rejection, or exactly nb random bits total if |F|=2^b.

sources.locator: §4.1 Discussion of costs, Table 4.1 and Remark 4.2, pp.37–39

items.title: Choosing a sum-check error budget
items.statement: For ε>0, a supplied field with |F|≥(sum_i d_i)/ε yields soundness at most ε.
items.strategy: Substitute in the soundness bound; field construction is not silently included.

items.title: Verifying formula counts over a supplied field
items.statement: For n≥1 and a formula with s nodes and variable occurrence counts t_i, its cube sum equals the satisfying-assignment count in F. Sum-check has perfect completeness, error at most min(1,sum_i t_i/|F|), and O(s+n) verifier field operations. For a supplied prime field F_p with p>2^n and 0≤K≤2^n, equality of the field sum and K is equivalent to equality of the integer count and K.
items.strategy: Sum Boolean values, use the occurrence bounds and formula-tree evaluator; injectivity for counts below p gives exactness. Large extension-field cardinality alone does not prevent characteristic wraparound.

items.title: The BLR linearity test over F_2
items.statement: For fixed f:F_2^n→F_2, choose independent uniform x,y and accept iff f(x)+f(y)=f(x+y). Distance is fraction of disagreements; linear functions are a·x, with no affine constant.
items.strategy: Define dot products mod 2 and the three-query test; random bits cost 2n. Include the Walsh-Hadamard truth-table encoding as terminology.

items.title: Characters and normalized Fourier coefficients
items.statement: For real h on F_2^n define χ_a(x)=(-1)^(a·x) and hhat(a)=2^-n sum_x h(x)χ_a(x).
items.strategy: Finite sums only; expectation is the uniform arithmetic mean. Distinguish real signs from arithmetic mod 2.

items.title: Character orthogonality, inversion and Parseval
items.statement: Uniform averages satisfy E χ_aχ_b=1 if a=b and 0 otherwise; h=sum_a hhat(a)χ_a; E hk=sum_a hhat(a) khat(a). In particular E h²=sum_a hhat(a)². Distinct linear Boolean functions disagree on exactly half the cube.
items.strategy: Pair x with x+e_j for a nonzero character. Sum characters over a to get the point delta identity, hence inversion; expand finite sums for Parseval and half-distance. No analytic Fourier theorem assumed.

items.title: The cubic Fourier identity for BLR
items.statement: For h=(-1)^f and BLR acceptance probability α, 2α-1=E h(x)h(y)h(x+y)=sum_a hhat(a)^3.
items.strategy: Expand three finite Fourier sums; character multiplication and independence kill all terms except equal indices.

items.title: BLR acceptance implies agreement with a linear function
items.statement: If BLR accepts with probability at least ρ>1/2, some linear a·x agrees with f on at least a ρ fraction. Equivalently rejection ε<1/2 guarantees distance at most ε. Linear functions have perfect completeness. Repeating the test k times independently rejects any function at distance greater than δ (0<δ<1/2) with probability at least 1-(1-δ)^k.
items.strategy: Parseval gives sum hhat²=1, so cubic sum≤max hhat; translate correlation at least 2ρ-1 into agreement at least ρ. Keep the signed maximum, not absolute value, to obtain linear rather than affine agreement. For repetition, multiply independent acceptance probabilities, each at most 1-δ.

items.title: Two-query linear self-correction
items.statement: For requested x and fixed oracle f, choose uniform y and output f(y)+f(x+y) over F_2.
items.strategy: This is pointwise correction with random queries, not an assertion that f(x) is already correct.

sources.locator: §18.4.1 Local decoding of Walsh-Hadamard code pp.364–365

items.title: Pointwise correctness under less than quarter noise
items.statement: If f has distance δ<1/4 from a linear ℓ, ℓ is unique and at every fixed x the corrector outputs ℓ(x) with probability at least 1-2δ>1/2. Uses two queries and n random bits.
items.strategy: Half-distance plus triangle inequality proves uniqueness. Each queried location is marginally uniform, so union bound ≤2δ; when both are uncorrupted, linearity proves the answer. Do not assume the two locations independent.

items.title: False: the sum-check verifier enumerates the cube
items.statement: False assertion: a sum-check verifier must evaluate g separately at all 2^n Boolean points.
items.strategy: Refute with the protocol resource theorem: one trusted point evaluation suffices; the prover may perform exponential work.

title: Arithmetization and the Sum-Check Protocol: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Interpolating a two-bit table over F_5
items.statement: For table f(0,0)=1,f(0,1)=2,f(1,0)=1,f(1,1)=4 over F_5, extension is 1+Y+2XY; evaluate at (2,3) to obtain 1 mod 5.
items.strategy: Expand the four Lagrange terms and check vertices and the requested value.

items.title: A complete sum-check transcript over F_101
items.statement: For g=2X³+XZ+YZ over F_101, H=12 and challenges 2,3,6 yield honest messages 8X³+2X+1, 34+Y, 16+5Z. Final value is 46.
items.strategy: Verify consistency 12,69,37 and final equality 46, all modulo 101; degree vector (3,1,1) gives error ≤5/101.

items.title: Correcting one corrupted table entry
items.statement: On F_2^3 take ℓ(x)=x_1 and corrupt only f(0). At each nonzero requested x, exactly y=0,x fail; success is 6/8. At x=0 the corrector always returns 0.
items.strategy: Enumerate the two bad query positions; compare δ=1/8 and bound 1-2δ=3/4. This is a concrete specialization of the source construction.

items.title: One point evaluation for an exponentially large cube
items.statement: Let g=product_i X_i over a supplied finite field. The cube has 2^n points and sum 1, while the sum-check verifier uses one n-multiplication evaluation and O(n) field work.
items.strategy: Check the unique nonzero Boolean summand and use degree bounds d_i=1; error ≤n/|F|. The example is about the verifier, not prover runtime.
